    Thresholds

    School · sets the row

    public by address + private
    When both count, use whichever is:

    Public school (by address) rank · Público 2025

    How the school row works

    There are two inputs behind this row: your zoned school for the address (this section) and a private school nearby (the “Private school” section below). When both are switched on, the lenient/strict toggle decides how they combine. Lenient (the default) uses whichever is better: strong + anything gives the green row, average + average or average + weak gives amber, weak + weak gives grey. Strict uses whichever is worse: strong + strong gives the green row, strong + average or average + average gives amber, weak + anything gives grey. Turning one of them off means colour follows only the one still on, and the toggle stops mattering; turn both off and every zone sits in the top row, coloured purely by the ocean.

    Your zoned school is whichever school your home address is assigned to — the school for your cluster (agrupamento), covering grades 5–9. A strong school from a different cluster nearby doesn’t count: under Portuguese enrolment rules, living in a catchment area only gives you priority for that catchment’s own school — elsewhere you’re competing for whatever places are left. A secondary school teaching grades 7–9 only counts as “yours” if it’s in the same cluster; a standalone school (with no cluster) or one belonging to a different cluster only counts where we’ve actually verified its catchment area — otherwise it’s just noted in the card.

    Rank comes from Público’s 2025 ranking of 9th-grade exam results across 1,161 schools — lower is better. The first slider sets the rank below which a school counts as “strong” (the top, green row). The second sets the rank above which it’s so weak the zone gets skipped entirely (grey). Anything in between is “average” (amber). The defaults aren’t arbitrary — they’re tied to the average exam grade (on a 1–5 scale, where 3 is a pass; the national average across público schools is 2.79, below a pass): “strong” is rank 200 or better, which works out to a grade of 3.2+ and the top 10% of schools nationally, where the average pupil passes both exams comfortably. “Grey” is anything worse than rank 450, a grade under 2.9, where the average pupil is failing. The “reset ranks” button puts these three sliders back to their defaults.

    A single year’s rank is noisy — público schools can jump by a hundred places or more from one edition to the next (the median shift is 115 places, and a quarter of schools move by more than 210). So colour is based on the worse of two years’ ranks, this edition and the previous one: a school only counts as “strong” if it cleared the threshold in both editions, and counts as “grey” if it fell below the grey line in either one. The card shows both years’ ranks.

    Each school’s card also shows a “context-adjusted rank” — the same ranking, but adjusted for the socioeconomic background of its pupils (Público publishes this as advantaged / average / disadvantaged). The raw rank tells you who’s in the classroom; the adjusted one tells you whether the school is doing better or worse than you’d expect given that intake. Colour is based on the raw rank, not the adjusted one.

    Upper secondary (grades 10–12) and international schools don’t affect colour at all. The upper-secondary slider only changes whether the card calls it “strong” or “weak” in the text; international schools have no slider — the card just shows the drive time to the nearest one. Upper secondary also uses the worse of two years’ ranks; the default is rank 120 or better out of 624, roughly a grade of 12.4/20 and the top 14% of schools.

    Private school · minutes by car · better of the two

    About private schools

    This is based on driving minutes to the nearest private school teaching the Portuguese curriculum. The first slider sets how many minutes counts as “nearby” (a strong result), the second sets the cutoff for “so-so”; beyond that there’s effectively no private option nearby (weak). This combines with your zoned school via the toggle in the “School” section above: lenient takes whichever is better (grey only if your zoned school is below the grey line and there’s no private school within the “so-so” cutoff), strict takes whichever is worse (grey if either your zoned school is below the grey line or there’s no private school within the cutoff — green only when your zoned school is strong and a private school is “nearby”). With just one switched on, colour follows that one alone. There’s no rank cutoff for private schools, because almost all of them already sit near the top of Público’s ranking (41 of the 47 with a 9th-grade rank are 200th or better) — the rank shown is just for reference. The one exception: a private school ranked worse than the grey line (the “grey zone” slider above) doesn’t count as a real option. There are three like that (Vagos, Braga, Amarante).

    Private schools with no rank at all — because they’ve had too few exam sitters to be ranked (Colégio Horizonte, CEI in São João da Madeira) or haven’t had any yet (Colégio Novo de Gaia and Colégio Ibérico de Gaia in Arcozelo, both opened in 2024) — still count as private schools. Colégio D. Duarte (Porto) has been removed: it closed in 2024. The table has a “Private” column and a “with private” filter; the card lists every private school within range along with its rank (secondary or 9th grade) or the reason it has none. International schools (full foreign curriculum) are handled separately — the card shows minutes to the nearest one on its own line.

    Dual Diploma means a pupil earns both the Portuguese school-leaving qualification and an American High School Diploma: they attend a Portuguese school and, in parallel, take six American courses online in English, usually starting around grade 8–10. In practice this is almost always the Academica programme. The private-school popup on the map shows whether a given school offers it (checked against Academica’s 2026 partner list and each school’s own website, as of 23 September 2026); the zone card flags it as “dual diploma” too.

    Ocean · sets the column

    to a beach
    About the ocean

    Driving minutes, with no traffic, to the nearest Atlantic beach. The first slider sets the cutoff for “close” (the left legend column), the second for “so-so” (the middle column); beyond that is “far” (the right column).

    Ocean only breaks ties within one school row — it never overrides the school result. A green zone with a distant beach still beats an amber zone with a beach right next door.

    Train · Porto

    card signals · far → hatching
    About the train

    Driving minutes to a station with frequent trains into Porto (the CP suburban lines) or the metro. The idea: a teenager gets driven to the station and takes the train from there on their own.

    This doesn’t affect colour — it just shows as a status light in the card, “ideal” from the first slider or “so-so” from the second. Past the second threshold, the map shows hatching for “far from the train”.

    About Porto

    Driving minutes to a fixed reference point in Porto (Boavista) — a stand-in for how close a place is to the city itself: the centre, friends, doctors. Trips into Porto are occasional, so this doesn’t affect colour either.

    Shown in the card as a status light: “ideal” or “so-so” depending on the sliders. Past the second threshold: “far from Porto” hatching.

    Minutes by car without traffic; add 10–30 % at rush hour. Thresholds live in the link and in this browser.

    How to read

    The map answers one question: “is a house in this zone worth a look, and how good is the location?” Every idealista zone around Porto is coloured by two things, always in the same order: first the school you’re zoned for, then the ocean. Train access and distance to Porto show up in the card as extra info, not as colour.

    Colour = school, then oceanThe row is set by your zoned public school and any nearby private school. With both switched on, a toggle decides how they combine: lenient uses whichever is better (one strong school is enough for the green row; it only goes grey if both are weak), strict uses whichever is worse (both need to be strong for green; either one being weak makes it grey). The column is set by distance to the ocean: close, so-so, or far. Darker is always better, and any green row beats any amber one.
    Grey = skip itThe school situation doesn’t clear the bar: in lenient mode, the zoned school is weak and there’s no good private option nearby; in strict mode, either one is weak. Whatever’s listed there, this zone is off the list.
    Hatching = a long driveThe train station or central Porto is further than the “so-so” cutoff. Not a dealbreaker, just a longer commute — the card says which one it is.
    Dotted edge = right on the lineThe number that decided the colour is basically sitting on a threshold — nudge a slider and the zone flips to the next colour. Worth checking the actual number in the card.
    Dots = zone spans two school clustersThe colour shown is for whichever cluster has the most homes in that zone; part of the zone may actually be zoned for a different school, sometimes a different colour. The card explains which part is which. For a specific house here, check the address with the school directly, not just the map.
    Private schools count tooThis looks at minutes to the nearest private school with a Portuguese curriculum, using the same “nearby” / “so-so” sliders as the train. Almost all private schools already rank near the top nationally, so their rank is shown just for reference, not as a cutoff. It combines with the zoned school through the same toggle described above: lenient uses whichever is better, strict whichever is worse. Turn off “private” on the left and the map goes back to public schools only; turn off both and colour is based on the ocean alone. The dots on the map mark the private schools themselves.
    Click a zoneA card opens with four status lights, a plain-English rundown of the school situation, the underlying facts, and a “Homes in this zone on idealista” button. The sliders on the left update the thresholds and the map recolours instantly.

    How to read it and where the numbers come from

    Zone = an idealista zone (the “Zonas” list in the site’s filter): an old parish (freguesia before 2013) or a 2013 union, exactly as idealista has them, so you can tick the zones in your house search. Boundaries come from the official CAOP 2012.1 / 2013 map (DGT). Minutes are measured from the centre of the zone’s main village (an OSM point) over the road network without traffic (OSRM); at rush hour real times are 10–30% longer.

    Colour is an order, not a score. School first, then ocean. Two legend rows — school strong or average — set by two inputs, your zoned público school and a private school nearby; a toggle decides whether to use whichever is better or whichever is worse of the two (lenient: at least one strong gives the green row, grey only when both are weak; strict: green only when both are strong, grey if either is weak; switching either input off means colour follows the one still on). Three columns — ocean close, so-so, far. A zone in the top row always beats any zone in the bottom row; within a row, the closer the ocean, the better. There are no weights or points being added up — the colour just reflects those two facts directly. Train and Porto aren’t part of the colour at all: they show as lights in the card, and if a zone is beyond the “so-so” threshold the map hatches it and says why. A dotted border means “borderline” — the deciding number (rank within 20 places, or minutes within 2) is right at a threshold, and a slider nudge would flip the zone to the next class.

    School: a child is placed at the cluster (agrupamento) school for their home address. Under Portuguese enrolment rules, living in a school’s catchment area gives you 6th priority for it; a strong school from another cluster nearby only has leftover places to offer, so it doesn’t count toward colour. Rank comes from Público’s 2025 ranking of 9th-grade exams (1,161 schools), but colour is based on the worse of two years’ ranks, this edition and the previous one, because a single year’s rank is noisy — the median shift between editions is 115 places. Strong means no worse than the threshold in both editions; grey means worse than the grey line in at least one. Público counts 9th-grade exams per building, so we use the best of the cluster’s own schools that teaches 9th grade — either the EB 2,3, or the cluster’s secondary school if it also teaches grades 7–9 (moving within a cluster only takes 2nd priority). A standalone secondary school (não agrupada, on the DGAE list) or one belonging to another cluster doesn’t count as “yours”: its 7th grade only admits by catchment area, at 6th priority if places are available, so it only counts toward colour where we’ve verified that catchment area (Esposende: Henrique Medina; Paços de Ferreira; Valadares: Ferreira Alves; Marco; Matosinhos: Zarco and Boa Nova; Ramalde: Clara de Resende) — elsewhere it’s just a note in the card. Where no catchment school has been established, we assume “so-so”, never “ideal”, unless the facts say otherwise. Next to the rank, the card also shows the “context-adjusted” rank — Público’s ranking de superação, the same rank adjusted for pupils’ family income and parents’ education — plus the intake itself; none of this affects colour. Upper secondary (secundário, 10–12) and international schools appear as facts in the card and don’t affect colour either.

    Private schools (added 21.09.2026): minutes to the nearest private school with the Portuguese curriculum, using two sliders — “nearby” (default 10 minutes, a strong result) and “so-so” (20); beyond that it counts as weak. This combines with the zoned público school through a toggle (added 23.09.2026): lenient, the default, uses whichever is better — at least one strong result gives the green row, grey only when both are weak; strict uses whichever is worse — green row only when both are strong, grey when either is weak. There are no rank cutoffs for private schools, because almost all of them already sit at the top of Público’s ranking (41 of the 47 with a 9th-grade rank are 200th or better); the rank shown is just for reference. The one exception is a private school ranked worse than the grey line, which doesn’t count as a real option — there are three of these (Vagos, Braga, Amarante). Private schools with no rank at all count too: Público doesn’t rank a school with too few exam sitters (in the 2025 edition, the smallest ranked school had 45 secondary exams and 38 at 9th grade) — this covers Colégio Horizonte, CEI, and Colégio Novo de Gaia and Colégio Ibérico de Gaia in Arcozelo (both opened in 2024, up to 9th grade, no exams yet). Colégio Cedros (boys only) is excluded, and so is Colégio D. Duarte in Porto, which closed in 2024. The “zoned school counts toward colour” and “nearby private school counts toward colour” checkboxes switch each input off: público-only gives you the map as it looked before 21.09; private-only colours purely by minutes to the nearest private school; both off colours by ocean only.

    Train: CP Urbanos do Porto stations (on the Aveiro, Braga, Guimarães and Marco lines) plus the metro; the narrow-gauge Vouga line and stations with regional-only trains (Barcelos, Viana) don’t count. The scenario: drive the teenager to the station, then they take the train from there. Ocean: the nearest Atlantic beach in OSM (river beaches don’t count). Porto: a fixed point in Boavista, used as a stand-in for Porto in general.
